section_1.title: Prerequisite: The Concept of Distributions
section_1.content: Briefly introduce that data can follow different shapes (Uniform, Skewed, etc.). Define a 'Sample Mean' as the average of a small group drawn from a population.
section_1.example: Visualizing a 'Die Roll' distribution (Uniform) vs. 'Height' distribution (Normal).

section_2.title: The Problem: The 'Wild' Population
section_2.content: Pose the question: What happens if we take samples from a population that isn't bell-shaped? Introduce the idea of collecting multiple sample means.
section_2.example: Imagine a population of squirrels with highly irregular, non-normal 'acorn-hoarding' behaviors.

section_3.title: The Experiment: The Magic of Aggregation
section_3.content: Visually demonstrate the process of taking 100 samples of size 'n', calculating the mean for each, and plotting them. Show the transition from the irregular population shape to a emerging Bell Curve.
section_3.example: Animated visualization: As the number of samples increases, the 'acorn-hoarding' averages settle into a perfect Normal Distribution.

section_4.title: Defining the Central Limit Theorem
section_4.content: Formalize the rule: As sample size (n) increases, the distribution of sample means will approach a Normal Distribution, regardless of the original population's shape. Emphasize the Mean and Standard Error.
section_4.example: A graphical overlay showing the narrow, tall bell curve of the sample means becoming more 'normal' as n goes from 5 to 30 to 100.

section_5.title: Real-World Application: Why it Matters
section_5.content: Explain that CLT is the foundation for Inferential Statistics. It allows us to calculate probabilities and confidence intervals even when we don't know the population's underlying distribution.
section_5.example: A quality control engineer testing thousands of circuit boards; even if individual board failures are random, the average failure rate follows a predictable pattern.
